text: ).3,5 Prehospital thrombolysis is feasible and reduces the time to give a thrombolytic, and short-term mortality.15 Five-year follow-up of one study16 has sug- gested that there is also a beneficial effect on long-term mortality. Percutaneous coronary interventions include balloon angioplasty, coronary stenting, and similar procedures. They are effective methods for reopening occluded coro- nary arteries,17 including in elderly patients,14 and can be used in acute coronary syndromes (primary PCI) and in stable coronary heart disease. However, specialist facilities are required, and availability may be limited. PCI is also safe and effective in patients in whom thrombolytics have failed to achieve adequate reperfusion (rescue PCI)18 and appears to be more effective than repeated thrombolytics or conservative therapy.19 Routine PCI after successful thrombolysis (facilitated PCI) has also been tried but ap- pears to provide no additional benefit and may be detri- mental, particularly if a full dose of thrombolytic has been given.20,21 Choice of reperfusion strategy is controversial and de- pends on patient factors and availability.12,17 PCI is more effective at opening occluded arteries than thrombolysis. Studies have shown that it is associated with lower mortal- ity and re-infarction rates both early and late after STE- MI,22 with benefit maintained up to 5 years,23 including in patients with cardiogenic shock.24 However, the advantage of PCI over thrombolysis appears to diminish as the delay to reperfusion increases; although some analyses25 have found that PCI is superior to thrombolysis irrespective of the time delay, others have suggested26 that thrombolysis may be preferred if the delay to PCI is 90 minutes or more, although this depends on patient characteristics.27 Guidelines3,4,7 therefore recommend that all patients with STEMI presenting within 12 hours should be reperfused. For those with a symptom duration of 3 hours or less, pri- mary PCI is preferred if it can be performed within 90 min- utes or the delay to treatment is less than 1 hour longer than for thrombolysis; PCI is also preferred if symptom dura- tion is greater than 3 hours, if the patient has cardiogenic shock or heart failure, or if thrombolytics are contra-indi- cated. Patients presenting more than 12 hours after symp- tom onset should generally only receive thrombolysis or PCI if there is evidence of ongoing ischaemia. The overall effectiveness of reperfusion is limited by per- sistent coronary occlusion, re-occlusion, and infrequent but serious bleeding complications (including intracranial haemorrhage with thrombolytics), and long-term resteno- sis after PCI.
